detected_issues.title: Numeric multipart bodies expose uninitialized process memory
detected_issues.body:
A numeric `body` takes the `Buffer(size)` path instead of being sent as its decimal value. On every Node version supported by this package, an application that forwards an untrusted numeric multipart field can make the client allocate that many bytes; on supported Node 0.8-era runtimes those bytes are uninitialized and are sent to the multipart recipient.

**Preconditions:** A multipart part body is a number, such as `multipart: [{body: 33554432}]`.

**Evidence:** `isChunked()` accepts a numeric body as a non-stream (`lib/multipart.js:32-40`). `build()` passes it to `add()` (`lib/multipart.js:78-87`), whose non-chunked branch calls `new Buffer(part)` (`lib/multipart.js:70-72`). Node interprets a number as an allocation length, not text. The resulting buffers are assigned to `self.body` (`request.js:1145-1149`) and written to the request (`request.js:554-563`). A local reproduction with `{body: 5}` produced five NUL bytes rather than `5`; the same runtime allocated 32 MiB for `{body: 33554432}`. `package.json:20` supports Node `>=0.8.0`, where `Buffer(size)` contains uninitialized memory.

**Impact:** A remote multipart recipient can receive process-memory residue from a client whose application accepts an attacker-controlled numeric field. This crosses the client-to-recipient trust boundary and cannot be recalled, so severity is high under the review policy. Modern Node versions zero-fill the allocation but still permit caller-controlled allocation and corrupt the payload.

**Fix:** Convert numeric part bodies to their decimal string before buffering or appending them, so each number is serialized as data rather than treated as a buffer length.

detected_issues.title: Quoted multipart boundaries produce invalid delimiters
detected_issues.body:
Valid caller-supplied `Content-Type` values with a quoted boundary generate delimiters containing the quote characters, so a compliant multipart recipient cannot parse the request. Boundary parameter names are case-insensitive as well; a differently cased parameter causes this code to append a second boundary parameter.

**Preconditions:** The caller supplies a valid multipart content type, for example `multipart/related; boundary="upload-1"` or `multipart/related; Boundary=upload-1`.

**Evidence:** `setHeaders()` finds and captures `boundary` with a case-sensitive search and `boundary=([^\\s;]+)` (`lib/multipart.js:53-61`). For the quoted form, that capture is `"upload-1"`; `build()` directly emits it in each `--<boundary>` delimiter (`lib/multipart.js:79-89`), while the header semantically declares `upload-1`. For `Boundary=...`, the search misses the existing parameter and appends another boundary (`lib/multipart.js:57-63`). A local recipient that unquotes and matches boundary parameters rejected both requests: the quoted case sent `--"upload-1"`, and the case-varied case contained two boundaries.

**Impact:** Requests using valid caller-provided content types fail at the selected recipient. The affected request can be corrected and retried, so this is low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Parse media-type parameters case-insensitively and unquote the boundary value before saving it; emit one canonical boundary parameter if absent.

detected_issues.title: Streamed multipart requests hang after redirects and auth retries
detected_issues.body:
A streamed multipart body is consumed by the first request and is then piped again after a redirect or deferred-auth retry. The second `ClientRequest` receives neither bytes nor `end`, so the request never reaches the redirected endpoint or invokes its callback. In deferred-auth mode, the full multipart payload is also sent before authentication.

**Preconditions:** A multipart part is a stream (which selects chunked mode) and the first response is a followed redirect or a 401 for `auth.sendImmediately: false`.

**Evidence:** A stream body selects a single `CombinedStream` (`lib/multipart.js:32-40`, `lib/multipart.js:66-72`, `lib/multipart.js:98-107`), which is piped unconditionally at send time (`request.js:537-553`). Redirect handling calls `request.init()` without the original multipart options (`lib/redirect.js:120-149`), so it does not rebuild this stream, but the next send pipes the exhausted `self._multipart.body` again (`request.js:551-553`). `CombinedStream` removes each stream as it is consumed and only starts its queue once (`node_modules/combined-stream/lib/combined_stream.js:64-68`, `89-96`, `150-174`). A local streamed upload that received a 302 emitted the redirect event but made no request to the Location and never called back. With deferred basic auth, the same path delivered the entire unauthenticated body before the 401 because multipart lacks the auth check used for forms (`request.js:543-553`).

**Impact:** Streamed uploads that require a redirect or challenge hang until caller timeout; deferred authentication also violates the caller's request not to send credentials-protected data before the challenge. The caller can abort and retry, making this low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Do not pipe multipart data before deferred authentication is sent, and retain enough multipart input state to construct a fresh stream for every redirect/auth retry (or reject non-replayable streamed multipart retries explicitly).

judge_reasoning: Issue 0 identifies the exact multipart numeric-body flaw: a number is passed to Buffer as an allocation size, causing non-zero/uninitialized memory to be transmitted to the multipart recipient. This is the CVE’s specific mechanism and data-exposure impact.

detected_issues.title: Chunked multipart skips required body validation
detected_issues.body:
Explicit chunked multipart input with a part that lacks `body` throws an internal `TypeError` instead of the documented multipart validation error. The documented object form permits callers to choose `chunked`, so this differs from the same invalid array input and makes invalid input handling depend on transfer mode.

**Preconditions:** The caller uses `multipart: {chunked: true, data: [...]}` (or supplies `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`) and one part has no `body` property.

**Evidence:** `isChunked()` sets `chunked` before entering the only missing-body check, which is guarded by `!chunked` (`lib/multipart.js:24-40`). `build()` then unconditionally appends `part.body` (`lib/multipart.js:81-90`). In the chunked branch, `add()` passes that `undefined` value to `CombinedStream.append()` (`lib/multipart.js:68-75`), which throws during request construction. The non-chunked form is tested and required to throw `Body attribute missing in multipart.` (`tests/test-errors.js:72-88`), and the README documents the `{chunked, data}` form (`README.md:740-746`).

**Impact:** A caller can reliably make its own request construction fail; no request reaches the remote server. This is contained and recoverable by correcting the input, and requires a caller that controls request options, so severity is info under the review policy.

**Fix:** Validate that every part has a `body` before deciding or building either transfer mode, then keep stream detection conditional on non-chunked mode. Add the explicit-chunked missing-body case to `tests/test-errors.js`.

detected_issues.title: Chunked multipart ends when a top-level body is also supplied
detected_issues.body:
A chunked multipart request that also has a top-level `body` is ended while its multipart stream is still writing. Later stream chunks then fail with `ERR_STREAM_WRITE_AFTER_END`, so the upload is truncated or the request fails.

**Preconditions:** The caller supplies a truthy `body` option and a multipart part whose body is a stream; the stream produces data after the request's first turn.

**Evidence:** Stream parts make the new serializer chunked and append the part stream to `CombinedStream` (`lib/multipart.js:37-43`, `lib/multipart.js:66-75`, `lib/multipart.js:81-92`). `Request.prototype.multipart()` leaves an existing `self.body` intact in chunked mode (`request.js:1142-1149`). On send, `end()` pipes the multipart stream, then the separate `if (self.body)` writes the old body and immediately ends the underlying request (`request.js:551-563`, `request.js:1350-1360`). Subsequent source data is forwarded through `Request.write()` to that ended request (`request.js:1341-1349`). A delayed readable stream with `body: 'EXTRA'` reproduces `ERR_STREAM_WRITE_AFTER_END`.

**Impact:** The affected caller's outbound request fails or loses multipart data. It is contained to one request and recoverable by retrying with a valid single body source; the caller must supply the conflicting options, so severity is info under the review policy.

**Fix:** Make multipart mutually exclusive with an existing top-level body: either reject that combination before starting the request, or clear/replace `self.body` when multipart takes ownership. Add a delayed-stream regression test for the chosen behavior.

judge_reasoning: Neither issue identifies multipart handling of a numeric body that is treated as a length and sends uninitialized non-zero memory. They concern missing part bodies causing local errors and conflicting top-level body plus streamed multipart causing truncation/failure.

cve_explanation: CVE-2017-16034 in https://github.com/soyuka/pidusage.git

detected_issues.title: Child-inclusive CPU samples recount prior child time
detected_issues.body:
With `{childrens: true}`, every sample after the first counts child CPU that was already included in an earlier sample. A process with no CPU activity in the current polling interval can therefore report substantial CPU use, which breaks consumers that use this option for monitoring or scheduling.

**Preconditions:** Linux caller samples the same PID more than once with `options.childrens` enabled.

**Evidence:** `cutime` and `cstime` are cumulative `/proc/<pid>/stat` counters (`lib/stats.js:63-64`). Line 71 adds their current total, but line 73 subtracts prior values only for the parent `utime` and `stime`; the prior child counters are retained in `history` at lines 82-83 but never used in the calculation. Thus the second sample adds all child CPU accumulated before that interval. With a 10-second interval, unchanged parent counters, and unchanged `cutime=1000` ticks at `CLK_TCK=100`, this code reports 100% although the correct interval usage is 0%.

**Impact:** A non-default option produces persistently inflated, potentially arbitrarily large CPU measurements for monitored processes. This is a broad but recoverable metrics error; the non-default option discounts severity to low.

**Fix:** When child accounting is enabled, add `(stat.cutime - previous.cutime) + (stat.cstime - previous.cstime)` rather than the current cumulative child total, treating missing prior values as zero.

detected_issues.title: Reused PIDs inherit CPU counters from an exited process
detected_issues.body:
A PID that is reused after the original process exits inherits that process's counters, so the next CPU result is an invalid cross-process delta. In the common case where the replacement has used less CPU, this returns a large negative CPU percentage.

**Evidence:** History is keyed only by PID at `lib/stats.js:43`; although the code parses each process's start time at line 66, it never compares it with `history.start`. Lines 73-75 subtract the old process's `utime`/`stime` and use its old sample uptime before replacing the history entry at lines 82-83. For example, after a sample at uptime 100 with `utime=stime=1000` ticks, a replacement of the same PID sampled at uptime 101 with `utime=3`, `stime=2` reports `(2-1000 + 3-1000) / 100 * 100 = -1995%`. An intervening read error also leaves the old entry intact (`lib/stats.js:49-51`).

**Impact:** Normal PID reuse makes monitoring report incorrect CPU for the replacement process until the caller explicitly clears the entry. This is a recoverable, contained metrics error; the exit/reuse timing discounts severity to low.

**Fix:** Treat a changed `/proc` start time as a new process and discard its prior PID history before calculating the delta. Clear history when a process read fails as well.

detected_issues.title: Exited Windows PIDs cause an uncaught WMIC parsing error
detected_issues.body:
A normal process-exit race can terminate a Windows caller rather than invoke its callback. WMIC returns a successful, nonempty `No Instance(s) Available.` response for a nonexistent PID, but this code assumes every successful response contains a second data row.

**Evidence:** Windows dispatches to `win` (`index.js:22,36-38`), which treats only empty stdout or a nonzero WMIC exit as an error (`lib/stats.js:146-158`). For WMIC's one-line no-instance response with exit code 0, `stdout.split(os.EOL)[1]` is `undefined`, so line 160 throws when it calls `.replace()`. A `wmic` substitute emitting `No Instance(s) Available.\r\r\n` and exiting zero reproduces an uncaught `TypeError`; `done` is never called. This occurs when a target exits between being selected and sampled.

**Impact:** Monitoring an exited PID can crash the Node process instead of reporting a routine sampling error. The failure is recoverable by restarting and requires the normal exit/sampling race, so severity is low.

**Fix:** Validate that WMIC produced a parseable result row before accessing it, and route no-instance or malformed output to `done(new Error(...))`.

detected_issues.title: First Windows sample reports lifetime CPU as one-second usage
detected_issues.body:
The first Windows sample treats a process's cumulative lifetime CPU time as CPU used in one second. Consequently, an ordinary first observation of a long-lived process can report an arbitrarily large percentage.

**Evidence:** With no history, the default values in line 169 make `total` equal the full WMIC `KernelModeTime + UserModeTime`, converted from 100-ns units at line 170. Lines 174-176 set the first-sample elapsed time to zero and then force it to one second; line 181 returns the resulting percentage. A mocked public Windows call with cumulative times of `1,000,000,000` and `2,000,000,000` returned `cpu: 30000`: 300 cumulative CPU seconds divided by one, despite a 10-day system uptime. The Linux path instead derives its initial interval from the process start time (`lib/stats.js:77`).

**Impact:** Every first sample of an existing Windows process can drive false alerts, throttling, or scheduling decisions. The result becomes delta-based after another successful call, so this is a broad transient metrics error and is low severity.

**Fix:** Establish a first-sample baseline without reporting an interval CPU value, or query the process creation time and use it to calculate a lifetime interval.

judge_reasoning: The CVE concerns command injection through PID handling, whereas all reported issues describe CPU-accounting inaccuracies or a Windows WMIC parsing crash during process-exit races. None identifies command execution via crafted input or the specific vulnerable instance.

detected_issues.title: Untrusted PIDs execute shell commands on ps platforms
detected_issues.body:
An application that passes an untrusted process identifier to `stat()` on a `ps` platform lets that caller run arbitrary shell commands as the Node process. For example, a PID of `1; <command>` terminates the intended `ps` invocation and executes `<command>`.

**Preconditions:** The application exposes a caller-controlled PID to this library on macOS, Solaris, FreeBSD, or AIX.

**Evidence:** The public wrapper forwards `pid` unchanged (index.js:6-14); those platforms dispatch to `ps` (index.js:17-24, index.js:32-38). `ps()` concatenates that value into a command passed to shell-backed `exec()` (lib/stats.js:96-103). A public-API proof with a mocked macOS platform and `1; : > /tmp/pidusage-marker` created the marker while returning normal process statistics.

**Impact:** An untrusted caller crosses into execution with the application's privileges. This is **high** under the reach/persistence policy: arbitrary command execution crosses a trust boundary and persists until the process or host is remediated.

**Fix:** Require a decimal integer PID before constructing platform commands. Prefer an argument-vector API such as `execFile`, or reject invalid input; do not concatenate caller data into a shell command.

detected_issues.title: Child-inclusive CPU samples recount prior child time
detected_issues.body:
On Linux, every later sample with `{ childrens: true }` adds all child CPU time accumulated since the parent started, rather than only the child time used since the prior sample. A parent that previously waited for a busy child continues to appear CPU-busy even while idle.

**Evidence:** The public Linux path preserves and forwards `options` (index.js:6-14, index.js:23, index.js:36-38). The parser stores `cutime` and `cstime` in history (lib/stats.js:57-64, lib/stats.js:79-80), but the total adds their current cumulative values without subtracting the prior values (lib/stats.js:68-72). In a reproduction, after a child had accumulated 78 ticks and exited, a later 1.1-second idle sample still reported 70.27% CPU; the counters had not increased and the correct interval value was about 0.9%.

**Impact:** Per-process monitoring that opts into child accounting receives persistently inflated CPU readings and can raise false alerts. This is **low**: it is contained to the monitored process and recoverable by correcting the next calculation/resetting history.

**Fix:** When child accounting is selected, add `(stat.cutime - previous.cutime) + (stat.cstime - previous.cstime)` to the parent CPU delta.

detected_issues.title: Reused PIDs inherit CPU counters from an exited process
detected_issues.body:
A PID that is reused after its original process exits inherits the previous process's CPU baseline. The next result can therefore be a negative or arbitrarily wrong CPU percentage for the new process.

**Evidence:** State is keyed only by PID (lib/stats.js:39-40, lib/stats.js:79-80). Although the parser reads each process's start time (lib/stats.js:57-64), it never compares it with `history.start` before subtracting the old `utime` and `stime` values (lib/stats.js:70-75). When the OS reassigns a monitored PID, the new counters are unrelated to that stored baseline.

**Impact:** A process monitor can misreport one newly started process until history is cleared, which is **low** under the reach/persistence policy: it is contained and callers can recover through `unmonitor()`.

**Fix:** Before using a PID's history, compare the saved and current process start times; discard the history when they differ.

detected_issues.title: First Windows CPU sample treats lifetime usage as one second
detected_issues.body:
The first Windows sample reports the process's lifetime CPU time as if it were consumed during one second. Long-lived but idle processes can therefore return arbitrarily large CPU percentages on the initial `stat()` call (and after `unmonitor()`), while a second sample is calculated from the real interval.

**Evidence:** With no history, the handler subtracts zero from WMIC's cumulative kernel and user times (lib/stats.js:119-120, lib/stats.js:158-167), sets elapsed time to zero, and then replaces that value with one second (lib/stats.js:169-172). It stores the baseline only after returning that result (lib/stats.js:174-177). A simulated response with 5 accumulated CPU seconds returned `cpu: 500` on its first call; a one-second later sample with 0.1 new CPU seconds returned the expected `cpu: 10`. This conflicts with the documented Windows calculation from time spent between calls (README.md:57-65).

**Impact:** Windows consumers can make a false alert or scheduling decision from every first observation. This is **low** under the reach/persistence policy: it affects the broad Windows caller set but clears on the next sample.

**Fix:** Treat the first successful response as a baseline and either return an explicit unavailable/zero CPU value, or obtain a real interval before returning a percentage. Do not substitute a one-second interval for missing history.

judge_reasoning: Issue 0 identifies the CVE’s command-injection instance: caller-controlled PID is concatenated into a shell-backed `exec()` command on ps-based platforms, allowing arbitrary command execution with the Node process’s privileges.

detected_issues.title: Static requests can read files outside the served directory
detected_issues.body:
Unauthenticated clients can use repeated dot segments to make the static route serve files outside the directory being hosted.

**Evidence:** `resourcePathname.replace(/\/\.\./, "").replace(/\.\.\//, "")` removes at most two matches before concatenation with `process.cwd()` (`lib/routes/statics.js:25-30`). A raw `GET /../../../.hostr-traversal-1842` left `../` in `filePath`; `fs.stat()` then succeeded and `fs.createReadStream()` returned a test file created in the parent directory (`lib/routes/statics.js:33-34`, `lib/routes/statics.js:62-65`). The normal CLI installs this handler before the fallback route (`lib/cli.js:96-100`). More segments can escape further.

**Impact:** Any remote caller can read every file readable by the hostr process, including source, configuration, and credentials outside the served directory. This crosses the service's filesystem access boundary and persists until files or permissions change, so severity is **high** under the review reach × persistence policy.

**Fix:** Decode and resolve the request pathname with a path-aware API, then reject it unless the resolved path remains within a resolved serving-root path. Do not attempt to strip traversal substrings.

detected_issues.title: OPTIONS requests for static files terminate the server
detected_issues.body:
An `OPTIONS` request for an existing static file ends the response and then crashes the hostr process when the static handler tries to set a header.

**Evidence:** The server's first request listener sends `200` and calls `res.end()` for every `OPTIONS` request, but it still registers `_handle` as a second listener (`lib/server.js:102-113`). The new handler does not exclude `OPTIONS`; after `fs.stat()` finds an existing path, it calls `res.setHeader('ETag', eTag)` (`lib/routes/statics.js:33-35`, `lib/routes/statics.js:51`). Reproduction with `OPTIONS /package.json` returned 200 to curl and then terminated Node with uncaught `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT` at line 51. The normal CLI mounts this handler for all paths (`lib/cli.js:96-100`).

**Impact:** Any network client can terminate the development server with one request for a known existing file. A restart recovers the service, so this is **medium** under the review reach × persistence policy (broad reach, recoverable disruption).

**Fix:** Ensure an OPTIONS response prevents middleware dispatch, or have the static handler immediately call `next()` for non-GET/HEAD methods before doing filesystem work.

detected_issues.title: Static assets cannot revalidate after their cache lifetime
detected_issues.body:
Unchanged assets are sent again after their cache lifetime instead of being revalidated with `304`, because the handler treats a future timestamp as an expiration test rather than using the file modification time.

**Evidence:** A `200` response sets `Last-Modified` to `Date.now() + _expirationTime`, not the stat result (`lib/routes/statics.js:59-60`). The `304` branch requires both a matching ETag and an `If-Modified-Since` value that is still in the future (`lib/routes/statics.js:47-56`). With `cacheExpiration: 2`, an initial GET supplied an ETag and future Last-Modified; the same validators returned 304 immediately, but returned 200 with the unchanged body after two seconds. A matching `If-None-Match` should be sufficient to validate an unchanged representation.

**Impact:** Every normally cached static asset is unnecessarily transferred again after its advertised freshness period. This wastes bandwidth and prevents conditional caching from working, but does not serve stale content, so severity is **low** under the review reach × persistence policy after discounting the bounded performance impact.

**Fix:** Set `Last-Modified` from the file's modification time and return 304 for a matching ETag (or correctly compare `If-Modified-Since` to that modification time). Include the cache metadata on the 304 response as well.

judge_reasoning: Issue 0 describes the directory-traversal flaw in the static-file route: insufficient removal of repeated ../ segments lets unauthenticated requests escape the served root and read arbitrary process-readable files. This is the same attack mechanism, impact, and vulnerable instance.

detected_issues.title: Directory URLs without a trailing slash return 500
detected_issues.body:
A request for an existing directory without a trailing slash returns `500` even when that directory has a valid `index.html`. For example, `/docs/` is served, while `/docs` tries to stream the directory itself and fails with `EISDIR`.

**Evidence:** The handler appends `index.html` only when the request-derived path ends in `/` (`lib/routes/statics.js:25-28`). `fs.stat` accepts a directory, then `fs.createReadStream(filePath)` attempts to read it (`lib/routes/statics.js:31`, `lib/routes/statics.js:60`). The non-`ENOENT` stream error path sends `500` (`lib/routes/statics.js:65-72`). The static handler is the root middleware, so ordinary requests reach it (`lib/cli.js:93-100`).

**Impact:** Any direct URL to a directory without its slash fails one request instead of serving or redirecting to its index. This is contained and recoverable by requesting the slash URL, so it is low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** After `stat`, distinguish directories from regular files. Redirect a directory request lacking a trailing slash to its slash form (or consistently resolve its index file), and only create streams for regular files.

judge_reasoning: The reported issue concerns an EISDIR error when requesting an existing directory without a trailing slash, producing a recoverable 500 response. It does not describe the CVE's specific vulnerability mechanism or instance.

cve_explanation: In the npm package semantic-release before version 17.2.3, secrets that would normally be masked by `semantic-release` can be accidentally disclosed if they contain characters that become encoded when included in a URL. Secrets that do not contain characters that become encoded when included in a URL are already masked properly. The issue is fixed in version 17.2.3.

detected_issues.title: URL-encoded Git credentials remain visible in release logs
detected_issues.body:
A token containing URL-reserved characters is left in the release log after this sanitizer has been installed. For example, with `GIT_CREDENTIALS=abcde+?[`, Node formats the authenticated repository URL as `https://abcde%2B%3F%5B@…`; applying this function leaves that string unchanged.

**Preconditions:** A selected credential contains a character that needs URL-component encoding, and semantic-release falls back to HTTPS credentials.

**Evidence:** `lib/hide-sensitive.js:16` applies `encodeURI` to the regex-escaped value, yielding `abcde%5C+%5C?%5C%5B`, rather than escaping the encoded value. It therefore matches neither the raw URL component `abcde%2B%3F%5B` nor the usual raw token. `lib/get-git-auth-url.js:94-100` builds an authenticated URL from `GIT_CREDENTIALS` after SSH authentication fails, and `index.js:56,69-73` logs that URL. The stdout/stderr hook installed at `index.js:242-246` is the only applicable masking path. A direct reproduction with Node's `url.format` produced `https://abcde%2B%3F%5B@example.test/r.git`, which this function returned unchanged.

**Impact:** A CI-log reader who is not allowed to use the Git credential can recover it and authenticate as the release job. Under the review policy this crosses a trust boundary; credential rotation is a supported recovery, so severity is high.

**Fix:** Generate the URI alternative from the unescaped value, then regex-escape that encoded string (and use the same URL-component encoding as the URL formatter), e.g. add an `escapeRegExp(encodeURIComponent(value))` alternative.

detected_issues.title: Prefixing secrets leave credential suffixes in output
detected_issues.body:
When one selected credential is a prefix of another, output containing the longer value is only partially hidden. With `FIRST_TOKEN=abcde` before `SECOND_TOKEN=abcde012345`, masking `SECOND_TOKEN` produces `[secure]012345`.

**Preconditions:** Two qualifying environment secrets are present in that enumeration order and the earlier value prefixes the later value.

**Evidence:** `lib/hide-sensitive.js:5-12` keeps `Object.keys(env)` order, and `lib/hide-sensitive.js:14-18` emits that order directly as regexp alternatives. JavaScript regex selection matches `abcde` before it can try `abcde012345`; replacement at `lib/hide-sensitive.js:20-21` then leaves the suffix. The transform is installed on stdout and stderr at `index.js:242-246`, so plugin or logger output containing the longer token reaches CI logs with that suffix intact.

**Impact:** A log reader learns part of a credential they are not authorized to use. This crosses a trust boundary and rotation can recover it, but the issue needs an uncommon prefix pair and a specific environment order; under the review policy that discount makes severity medium.

**Fix:** Sort replacement values longest-first before building the alternation, so a matching longer secret always wins.

It specifically attributes the flaw to incorrect encoding/regex construction in hide-sensitive.js.

detected_issues.title: URL-encoded Git credentials remain visible in release logs
detected_issues.body:
When an HTTPS Git credential contains a character encoded by `url.format`, the normal release banner prints the encoded credential because the new redactor searches only for the raw environment value. For example, `GIT_CREDENTIALS=build:pa/ssword` becomes `https://build:pa%2Fssword@…`; the sanitizing regex does not match it.

**Preconditions:** HTTPS fallback is used and `GIT_CREDENTIALS` is the sole configured Git credential.

**Evidence:** `get-git-auth-url.js:94-99` supplies the environment value as URL auth, and `get-git-auth-url.js:19-28` serializes it with `url.format`. `hide-sensitive.js:14-16` constructs alternatives only from the raw value, then returns unmatched output unchanged. `index.js:56` stores the resulting URL and `index.js:69-73` sends it to the normal logger; the stdout/stderr hook at `index.js:242-246` invokes the inadequate sanitizer.

**Impact:** The release credential is written to normal CI output, where a log reader can recover it. This crosses the credential/log-reader trust boundary and remains available for the log retention period, so the severity is high.

**Fix:** Match every serialized representation that core can log, including percent-encoded URL auth. Build regex alternatives from the raw value and its encoded value, escaping each representation after encoding.

detected_issues.title: Prefixing secrets leave credential suffixes in output
detected_issues.body:
If one sensitive environment value starts with another that appears earlier in the environment, redaction replaces only the shorter value and leaves the longer credential's suffix in output. With `SHORT_TOKEN=abcde` before `LONG_TOKEN=abcdeXYZ`, output `Bearer abcdeXYZ` becomes `Bearer [secure]XYZ`.

**Evidence:** `hide-sensitive.js:5-12` collects qualifying values in `Object.keys(env)` order. `hide-sensitive.js:14` preserves that order in regex alternation, so it produces `abcde|abcdeXYZ`; regex matching selects the first alternative at the same offset. `hide-sensitive.js:15-16` writes the partially replaced output. The entry point defaults to `process.env` and installs this redactor for stdout/stderr at `index.js:242-246`.

**Impact:** A suffix of a release secret is retained in normal release logs. This disclosure is bounded to logs from environments that have overlapping secret values, but it persists for the log retention period; severity is medium.

**Fix:** Order alternatives from longest value to shortest before building the regex, so a complete secret always wins at a shared starting offset.

detected_issues.title: Non-string sensitive environment values abort API startup
detected_issues.body:
A programmatic caller can supply the documented `env` object with a non-string sensitive value, causing release startup to throw before configuration is loaded. For example, `{MY_TOKEN: 123456}` reaches `123456.trim()` and raises `TypeError`.

**Evidence:** The JS API documents `config.env` only as an `Object` at `docs/developer-guide/js-api.md:94-101`. The entry point passes it directly to `hideSensitive` at `index.js:242-246`. The name filter in `hide-sensitive.js:5-12` invokes `.trim()` without checking the value type.

**Impact:** One trusted API caller configuration prevents that release invocation from starting. The failure is contained and resolved by supplying a string; this discount makes severity info.

**Fix:** Only trim and redact string values (or coerce values consistently before processing).

detected_issues.title: JSON objects can bypass array schemas by spoofing constructor.name
detected_issues.body:
A JSON request can make a plain object pass an array schema. Supplying an own `constructor` member shadows `Object.prototype.constructor`, and the comparison trusts its attacker-controlled `name`.

**Preconditions:** The application validates caller-controlled JSON against a schema containing an empty array/object constructor pattern.

**Evidence:**
```js
const jpv = require('./index');
const payload = JSON.parse('{"items":{"constructor":{"name":"Array"}}}');
jpv.validate(payload, { items: [] }); // true
Array.isArray(payload.items);          // false
```
For an empty `[]` pattern, traversal falls through to `compareCommon` (`index.js:216-240`). That comparison accepts the value when `value.constructor.name` equals the pattern constructor name (`index.js:117-123`). Both standard and strict validation use this path (`index.js:253-264`). The documented constructor pattern says `[]` denotes an array (`README.md:222-263`). This is CVE-2019-19507 (GHSA-rh46-3fgc-mvrf).

**Impact:** An untrusted request crosses the validator's type boundary and can bypass downstream array/object validation. This is high under the review policy: the caller can repeatedly cause an application to accept a value its schema denies, and the CVE reproduction confirms all preconditions.

**Fix:** Compare the actual constructors by identity (or use `Array.isArray`/prototype checks) rather than reading a value-controlled `constructor.name` property.

detected_issues.title: Empty nested objects bypass required schema fields
detected_issues.body:
A present but empty nested object bypasses every required field in its nested schema. The same bypass applies in strict mode.

**Evidence:**
```js
const { validate } = require('./index');
const input = { account: {} };
const schema = { account: { role: '(string)' } };
validate(input, schema);                    // true
validate(input, schema, { mode: 'strict' });// true
```
The forward pass sees no own fields in `account` (`index.js:207-208`). In the reverse existence pass, recursion only occurs when the second object has keys (`index.js:230-235`); there the second object is the empty input account. It instead calls `compareExistence` on the two defined containers, which returns true without visiting `role` (`index.js:237-240`, `index.js:166-181`). Both modes share that existence pass (`index.js:253-264`). `?` is the documented mechanism for allowing absent values; `'(string)'` is not optional (`README.md:368-402`).

**Impact:** A caller can omit required nested request data while receiving a successful schema validation. This crosses the validator's input boundary and is recoverable by correcting the payload, so it is high under the review policy.

**Fix:** During the schema-to-input existence traversal, recurse into a nested object whenever the schema side has fields (or either side has fields), so required leaves are checked even when the input container is empty.

detected_issues.title: `[exist]` accepts null, false, and empty strings
detected_issues.body:
`[exist]` accepts values that its expression definition says are empty, so callers cannot use it to require a meaningful supplied value.

**Evidence:**
```js
const { validate } = require('./index');
validate({ value: null }, { value: '[exist]' }); // true
validate({ value: false }, { value: '[exist]' }); // true
validate({ value: '' }, { value: '[exist]' }); // true
```
The expression table defines `exist` as excluding empty strings, `false`, `null`, and `undefined` (`expressions.js:8-11`). The logical-pattern branch coerces every value through `String` and applies `/.*/` (`index.js:69-78`), so all three values match. The public validator reaches that branch for a supplied primitive field (`index.js:197-201`, `index.js:253-255`).

**Impact:** A request can satisfy an `[exist]` constraint with null, false, or an empty string. This affects one validation result and is recoverable by resubmitting valid data, so it is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Handle the documented empty values before string coercion, or define `[exist]` with explicit nonempty semantics.

detected_issues.title: JSON keys named hasOwnProperty make validation throw
Root object and array schemas accept the wrong container type
detected_issues.body:
Root constructor patterns do not validate the root value's type. For example, a scalar or array can pass an object pattern, including in strict mode.

**Evidence:**
```js
const { validate } = require('./index');
validate([], {});                    // true
validate([], {}, { mode: 'strict' });// true
validate({}, []);                    // true
```
The documented constructor patterns distinguish `{}` from `[]` (`README.md:222-263`), and `compareCommon` contains a constructor check (`index.js:116-125`). `iterate` invokes that check only when the pattern is primitive (`index.js:197-202`); object/array root patterns only cause property traversal (`index.js:207-245`). Empty roots therefore never reach the comparison in either validation mode (`index.js:253-264`).

**Impact:** Callers that validate a root JSON value can accept the wrong container type. This affects one validation result and is recoverable by resubmitting data, so it is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Compare the root value against an object/array constructor pattern before traversing its properties.

judge_reasoning: Issue 0 identifies the constructor.name spoofing flaw that lets attacker-controlled JSON objects satisfy array constructor schemas, producing the validator type-bypass described by CVE-2019-19507.

detected_issues.title: Merging JSON with __proto__ still pollutes Object.prototype
detected_issues.body:
An application that merges attacker-controlled parsed JSON still pollutes `Object.prototype`. `flags.js` does not define the capability used here, so in normal calls both operands of the comparison are `undefined` and an own `__proto__` key is accepted.

**Evidence:** `Object.keys(source)` includes the own enumerable key made by `JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"polluted":true}}')` at `lib/reduce_object.js:21`. Because `behaviors.allowDangerousObjectKeys` is absent from `flags.js:2-7`, the test at `lib/reduce_object.js:23` evaluates `undefined !== undefined` as false, and line 28 recursively merges through `acc["__proto__"]`, which is the inherited `Object.prototype` of the ordinary target. The public immutable path reaches this code through `immutable.js:18`, `mutable.js:20`, `merge.js:37`, and `adapters/object.js:20`. Reproduction with `require('./')(JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"polluted":true}}'))` leaves `({}).polluted === true`.

**Impact:** Any service which merges request JSON can let an untrusted caller alter the prototype inherited by unrelated objects in the Node process. This crosses a trust boundary and persists for the process lifetime, so severity is high under the review policy.

**Fix:** Define `allowDangerousObjectKeys` as an unguessable behavior capability in `flags.js` and preserve the merge context when invoking the reducer (for example, `reduceObject.call(this, to, from, merge)`). Default behavior must skip `__proto__`; only a caller presenting that capability should be allowed to copy it.

judge_reasoning: The issue identifies the CVE's prototype-pollution flaw: attacker-controlled JSON containing an own `__proto__` property is recursively merged into an ordinary target, modifying `Object.prototype`. It names the specific reducer path and demonstrates process-wide prototype pollution.

detected_issues.title: Structured schemas accept values that omit required descendants
detected_issues.body:
Structured schemas do not reject empty or primitive values that omit required descendants. This affects nested object schemas and every element of a one-element array schema in both modes, so a caller that relies on `validate()` to reject malformed request data can accept values outside its schema.

**Evidence:** `jpv.validate({profile: {}}, {profile: {id: '(number)'}})` returns `true` in standard and strict mode although `id` is required. The recursion condition only descends when the *schema* has keys (`index.js:260-267`), but `iterate()` then enumerates only properties of the actual value (`index.js:224-275`); an empty object therefore never invokes the required-field comparison. The same flaw affects array elements: `jpv.validate({users: [{id: 1}, {}]}, {users: [{id: '(number)'}]})` and `jpv.validate({users: [null]}, {users: [{id: '(number)'}]})` both return `true` in either mode. The array branch recurses on each element (`index.js:243-257`), but it does not establish that an element satisfies its object schema before this value-driven traversal. The initial existence pass is additionally bounded by the one-element schema array (`index.js:246-253`, `index.js:284-290`), and strict mode repeats it without correcting the omission (`index.js:299-306`). This contradicts strict mode's same-hierarchy requirement (`README.md:269-271`) and the array documentation's promise that the first nested pattern validates every object (`README.md:434-437`).

**Impact:** A malformed value crosses the validation boundary for one caller request. It is recoverable by rejecting the request after a corrected validation result, so this is low severity under the review reach/persistence policy.

**Fix:** Traverse schema properties when checking required fields, including for every input array element, and reject a value whose container type cannot satisfy a nonempty object schema before recursing. Apply that invariant in both modes.

detected_issues.title: JSON keys named hasOwnProperty make validation throw
detected_issues.body:
A normal JSON property named `hasOwnProperty` makes `validate()` throw instead of returning its documented boolean result. An untrusted request body can therefore turn validation into an uncaught request failure when applications pass its parsed object to this library.

**Evidence:** `jpv.validate(JSON.parse('{"hasOwnProperty":1}'), {})` throws `TypeError: value.hasOwnProperty is not a function` in standard and strict mode. `iterate()` enumerates the attacker-controlled key and invokes `value.hasOwnProperty(property)` directly (`index.js:227-229`). It also directly invokes `pattern.hasOwnProperty(property)` for the counterpart (`index.js:231-235`). Both validation modes route ordinary objects through this function (`index.js:284-306`). Standard mode explicitly permits properties absent from the pattern (`README.md:269-271`), and the API promises a boolean result (`README.md:47`).

**Impact:** One validation attempt fails rather than yielding valid or invalid; retrying repeats it, and no data is altered. This is low severity under the review reach/persistence policy.

**Fix:** Use `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(value, property)` and the same form for `pattern`, so ordinary JSON keys cannot shadow the membership check.

detected_issues.title: RegExp patterns return match results instead of booleans
detected_issues.body:
A documented direct `RegExp` field pattern can cause `validate()` to return a match array or `null`, not a boolean. Callers that compare the result to `true` or serialize it receive the wrong API value.

**Evidence:** `jpv.validate({key: 'A-8'}, {key: /^[A-Z]-[0-9]$/})` returns `['A-8', ...]`, and the nonmatching input returns `null`, in both modes. The direct-RegExp branch returns `String(value).match(pattern)` without converting it to a boolean (`index.js:47-51`); `compareStandard` and `compareStrict` return that value unchanged (`index.js:141-148`, `index.js:158-166`), and the final traversal result escapes from each validator (`index.js:284-306`). Direct RegExp field patterns are documented (`README.md:167-180`) and `validate()` promises `true` or `false` (`README.md:47`).

**Impact:** The result for one validation call violates the public API contract but remains truthy/falsy in conditionals. It is contained and transient, so this is info severity under the review reach/persistence policy.

**Fix:** Convert the direct-RegExp result to a boolean, for example `pattern.test(String(value))`, while resetting or avoiding stateful `g`/`y` regular-expression state as needed.

detected_issues.title: The [exist] pattern accepts excluded empty values
detected_issues.body:
`[exist]` accepts `null`, `false`, and the empty string even though its defined-pattern contract excludes them. A caller using the pattern to require a populated value can therefore accept an invalid request field in either validation mode.

**Evidence:** `jpv.validate({x: null}, {x: '[exist]'})`, the analogous `false` input, and the empty-string input all return `true` in standard and strict mode. The expression definition says `[exist]` accepts anything except empty string, `false`, `null`, or `undefined`, but defines it as `/.*/` (`expressions.js:8-11`). The logical-pattern branch coerces the value to a string and matches that expression (`index.js:69-79`), so `"null"`, `"false"`, and `""` all match. Both validators reach that comparison path (`index.js:284-306`).

**Impact:** A malformed scalar field crosses a caller's validation boundary for one request. It is recoverable by rejecting the request after a corrected validation result, so this is low severity under the review reach/persistence policy.

**Fix:** Implement the stated `[exist]` predicate before string coercion, or use an expression and comparison path that reject `null`, `false`, and `""` explicitly.

judge_reasoning: Issue 1 identifies the validation crash caused by attacker-controlled JSON overriding `hasOwnProperty`, producing a denial of service through the same vulnerable membership-check calls in `iterate()`.

detected_issues.title: Merging JSON input can pollute Object.prototype
detected_issues.body:
Merging JSON input with an own `__proto__` key changes the process-wide `Object.prototype`. An application that passes a request body to the normal `deeply(value)` API can therefore let a remote caller supply inherited properties to unrelated objects until restart.

**Preconditions:** The application deep-merges an attacker-controlled JSON object.

**Evidence:** `immutable()` starts the public merge with an undefined target (`immutable.js:16-18`), so `merge()` creates a normal object for an object source (`merge.js:28-37`, `merge.js:91-112`) and dispatches to `objectAdapter` (`adapters/object.js:17-22`). `Object.keys(JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"polluted":"yes"}}'))` contains `__proto__`. At this line, `acc[key]` resolves to the target's inherited `Object.prototype`; because that and the payload value are both objects, the recursive call retains and writes into `Object.prototype`. Reproduction: `require('./')(JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"polluted":"yes"}}')); ({}).polluted` returns `"yes"`.

**Impact:** An unauthenticated input that an application merges can alter shared prototype state and affect unrelated requests and security decisions. It persists until the process restarts. Per the review policy, this crosses a trust boundary with recoverable persistence, so severity is high.

**Fix:** Skip `__proto__` before reading or assigning `acc[key]` (and add a JSON-payload regression test that asserts `({}).polluted` remains undefined).

judge_reasoning: The issue identifies the CVE's prototype-pollution flaw: attacker-controlled JSON containing an own __proto__ key is deep-merged, causing writes into Object.prototype and process-wide inherited-property pollution.

detected_issues.title: Context property names execute before the requested expression
detected_issues.body:
A browser caller that uses a fixed, trusted expression but builds `context` from request JSON can have a property name execute in the page origin. For example, `saferEval('1', JSON.parse('{"x;this.pwned=1;//":0}'))` emits `var x;this.pwned=1;// = ...` before `return 1`; the injected assignment runs with the host global as `this`.

**Preconditions:** The browser application passes attacker-controlled context property names while its `code` argument remains trusted.

**Evidence:** `allow` accepts the key because `isIdentifier` is only a blacklist (`src/common.js:11-14`, `src/common.js:66-71`). `runInContext` then concatenates every accepted key directly into a `var` declaration and parses it through `Function` (`src/browser.js:43-49`). That dynamic function has no strict-mode directive and `.call(null, ...)` therefore gives it the browser global object. Browser bundlers select this newly added implementation (`package.json:18-21`).

**Impact:** The property name crosses from untrusted data into executable page-origin JavaScript, so it can read page data or act as the user. This is **medium** under the review policy: it crosses a trust boundary and can have permanent effects, discounted because it requires the documented non-default integration of deserializing hostile data into `context`.

**Fix:** Do not form source from context keys. At minimum, validate names against a complete, anchored JavaScript identifier grammar and quote property lookups with `JSON.stringify`; preferably avoid generated declarations entirely.

judge_reasoning: The reported issue is code injection through attacker-controlled context property names concatenated into generated `var` declarations in the browser implementation. The CVE specifically concerns escaping the safer-eval sandbox via `constructor` properties. Although both can execute arbitrary JavaScript, they use different mechanisms and identify different flaws.

detected_issues.title: Browser expressions execute with the embedding page's global object
detected_issues.body:
Untrusted expressions evaluated by the browser entry point can read and modify the embedding page without any capability in `context`. For example, `saferEval('this.document.cookie')` evaluates with `this === window`; `(function () {}).constructor('return this')()` likewise returns `window` despite the local `Function` binding.

**Evidence:** `runInContext` concatenates the expression into a `Function` body at `src/browser.js:42-47` and invokes it with `.call(null, __context)` at `src/browser.js:49`. A `Function` body does not inherit the module's strict mode, so a null receiver becomes the browser global object. The context only shadows bare identifiers such as `window`, `document`, and `Function` (`src/common.js:22-34`); it does not constrain `this` or function-literal constructors. The browser package mapping makes this implementation the normal browser entry point (`package.json:18-21`).

**Impact:** An application that uses this evaluator for tenant- or user-supplied expressions grants that input the application's browser-origin privileges, including page data and same-origin requests, rather than its intended selected context. This crosses the application's expression trust boundary and has high, recoverable impact under the review policy.

**Fix:** Do not claim or implement a sandbox using same-realm `Function`; execute untrusted browser code in an isolated realm/worker with a message-only API, or remove this entry point. At minimum, do not invoke generated source with the host global as `this`, but that alone cannot make same-realm evaluation safe.

detected_issues.title: Context property names inject statements into browser evaluation
detected_issues.body:
A context object with an attacker-controlled property name can execute statements before the supplied expression. For example:

```js
const context = {}
context['x;this.__injected=1;//'] = null
saferEval('0', context)
```

This produces a generated declaration equivalent to `var x;this.__injected=1;// = __context[...]`; the comment suppresses the rest of the generated line.

**Preconditions:** The caller accepts untrusted keys in the public `context` object. This is distinct from accepting untrusted expression text: a trusted expression can be preceded by injected code.

**Evidence:** `isIdentifier` only rejects a limited blacklist (`src/common.js:11-14`), so the example key passes it and `allow` copies it into the internal context (`src/common.js:66-70`). `runInContext` interpolates every resulting key unescaped into `var <key>` and into a single-quoted property lookup before executing the body (`src/browser.js:44-49`). The browser mapping exposes that code to bundled browser users (`package.json:18-21`).

**Impact:** Configuration or request data that supplies context keys can execute as the embedding page, not merely provide a named value. This crosses the expression/configuration trust boundary. The README advises callers not to deserialize hostile context (`README.md:48`), so the documented mitigation discounts the otherwise high, recoverable impact to medium under the review policy.

**Fix:** Validate keys against the complete JavaScript IdentifierName grammar (and reject reserved words), and use `JSON.stringify(key)` for the generated property access. Prefer avoiding generated declarations entirely.

judge_reasoning: Issue 0 identifies the constructor-based sandbox escape: a function literal's `.constructor` yields a host `Function`, allowing supplied expressions to obtain the browser global and execute arbitrary generated code outside the intended context. This is the CVE's constructor-property arbitrary-code-execution flaw.

cve_explanation: Fast-csv is an npm package for parsing and formatting CSVs or any other delimited value file in node. In fast-cvs before version 4.3.6 there is a possible ReDoS vulnerability (Regular Expression Denial of Service) when using ignoreEmpty option when parsing. This has been patched in `v4.3.6` You will only be affected by this if you use the `ignoreEmpty` parsing option. If you do use this option it is recommended that you upgrade to the latest version `v4.3.6` This vulnerability was found using a CodeQL query which identified `EMPTY_ROW_REGEXP` regular expression as vulnerable.

detected_issues.title: The parse package cannot compile because isEmptyRow is undefined
detected_issues.body:
`Parser.ts` calls `RowParser.isEmptyRow`, but `RowParser` defines no such static member. The parse package's TypeScript build therefore fails with TS2339 and emits no package output. If it is transpiled despite that error, callers using the public `ignoreEmpty` option instead get a `TypeError` when a row is parsed.

**Evidence:** `Parser.parseRow` calls the missing member at `packages/parse/src/parser/Parser.ts:80`; the complete `RowParser` class has no `isEmptyRow` declaration (`packages/parse/src/parser/RowParser.ts:7-80`). `packages/parse/tsconfig.json:2-10` compiles `src`, while the shared build config enables `noEmitOnError` (`tsconfig.build.json:11`).

**Impact:** This blocks every build and release of `@fast-csv/parse`. By the review severity policy, the broad but recoverable build failure is **medium**.

**Fix:** Add the intended empty-row predicate to `RowParser` (or implement it in `Parser`) before calling it, and retain the expected `ignoreEmpty` semantics.

detected_issues.title: Split comment CRLF delimiters emit a spurious empty row
detected_issues.body:
When a comment-enabled stream receives a comment line whose CRLF delimiter is split between chunks, the parser consumes the terminal `\r` and treats the following `\n` as an empty CSV row. For example, writing `# comment\r` and then ending with `\na,b\r\n` emits `[]` before `['a', 'b']`; the same unsplit bytes emit only `['a', 'b']`.

**Preconditions:** Parsing uses `comment`, and a CRLF delimiter falls on a chunk boundary after a comment.

**Evidence:** `parseWithComments` calls `advancePastLine` and discards the consumed comment at `packages/parse/src/parser/Parser.ts:54-65`. `Scanner.advancePastLine` accepts and consumes a final standalone `\r` even when `hasMoreData` is true (`packages/parse/src/parser/Scanner.ts:71-81`). The next chunk's orphaned `\n` is then accepted by `RowParser` as a row delimiter and pushed as an empty row (`packages/parse/src/parser/RowParser.ts:21-36`; `packages/parse/src/parser/Parser.ts:76-83`).

**Impact:** A normal streamed CSV upload can gain a record and shift downstream row handling. By the review severity policy, this is a contained, recoverable parsing error, discounted because comments are opt-in: **low**.

**Fix:** When `advancePastLine` finds a terminal `\r` with more data expected, preserve it rather than consuming it, matching `RowParser`'s CRLF-boundary handling.

detected_issues.title: Whitespace-only final CSV records are silently dropped
detected_issues.body:
A final record containing only whitespace is silently dropped when `ignoreEmpty` has its default `false` value. `parse('   \t', false)` returns no rows and retains the text in `line`, whereas `parse('   \t\n', false)` emits the record. Stream flush only processes returned rows, so the retained final record is lost.

**Evidence:** `Parser.parseRow` returns before delegating to `RowParser` when `nextNonSpaceToken` is absent (`packages/parse/src/parser/Parser.ts:72-75`). Thus whitespace at EOF remains unconsumed in the result (`packages/parse/src/parser/Parser.ts:42-49`), and `CsvParserStream._flush` processes only `rows` (`packages/parse/src/CsvParserStream.ts:90-111`). The documented `ignoreEmpty` option is the opt-in behavior for discarding whitespace-only columns (`documentation/docs/parsing/options.md:85-92`), and the default is false (`packages/parse/src/ParserOptions.ts:32`).

**Impact:** A CSV row is omitted based solely on whether its final newline is present, corrupting one imported record. By the review severity policy, this is contained and recoverable: **low**.

**Fix:** On the final parse pass, let `RowParser` consume a whitespace-only suffix so that default behavior emits the row; apply `ignoreEmpty` only after that row is formed.

judge_reasoning: None of the issues identifies catastrophic regular-expression backtracking or denial of service in the ignoreEmpty empty-row check. They describe a missing method/build failure, CRLF comment parsing error, and dropped whitespace-only final row.

detected_issues.title: Quoted CSV fields can trigger catastrophic empty-row regex backtracking
detected_issues.body:
With `ignoreEmpty: true`, a CSV field can make parsing block the Node.js event loop for seconds. A quoted field containing repeated `,` plus whitespace groups and a final non-matching character reaches the empty-row regex as literal field data, so an input such as `"," + " ".repeat(100) + "," + " ".repeat(100) + "," + " ".repeat(100) + "X\n"` triggers exponential backtracking.

**Preconditions:** The consumer enables the non-default `ignoreEmpty` option and parses attacker-controlled CSV.

**Evidence:** `parseRow` applies `EMPTY_ROW_REGEXP` to `row.join('')` at `packages/parse/src/parser/Parser.ts:73-84`. The pattern at `Parser.ts:7` has adjacent variable-length whitespace terms in its repeated comma group. A quoted parser preserves comma and whitespace as a column's data (`packages/parse/src/parser/column/QuotedColumnParser.ts:45-87`), so the input reaches that regex. A reproduction through `Parser.parse` on Node 24.18 took about 1.4 seconds for three 100-space groups; four groups exceeded seven seconds. The public stream passes incoming bytes to this parser synchronously in `_transform` (`packages/parse/src/CsvParserStream.ts:74-86`).

**Impact:** A caller that accepts CSV uploads can stall its process for a few hundred bytes; Node cannot process other requests while this synchronous parse runs. This is a broad but recoverable denial of service. The non-default option discounts it one tier under the review policy: **low**.

**Fix:** Do not serialize parsed fields into a backtracking regex to test emptiness. Test each parsed column with a linear whitespace-only predicate (or an equivalent linear scan), and retain quoted delimiter characters as data.

detected_issues.title: Method-override headers can block the event loop quadratically
detected_issues.body:
A remote caller can keep a Node worker busy by sending an ordinary POST with `X-HTTP-Method-Override: A` followed by a long run of spaces and `B`. The default configuration selects that header and examines POSTs. The header getter runs the vulnerable split before the invalid value is rejected; `/ *, */` greedily scans and backtracks over the remaining spaces for every possible start when no comma exists. On Node 24, 16,000 spaces take about 200 ms in this middleware, and 64,000 take about 3.2 s. The request handler cannot serve other requests while this synchronous work runs.

**Evidence:** The default getter is `X-HTTP-Method-Override` and POST is allowed by default (`index.js:48-55`). Header values reach `split(/ *, */)` at `index.js:112-121`, while only `val[0]` is used later (`index.js:68-71`) and method validation follows the split (`index.js:73-76`). Replacing the split with `indexOf(',')` plus `trim()` makes the scan linear and returns only the consumed first value.

**Impact:** Any client able to reach middleware using the default header can degrade service for all requests on that Node worker. This is **low** under the review policy: the outcome is broad but recoverable, and Node's maximum request-header size bounds each individual request (16 KiB by default on current Node; deployments may raise it).

**Fix:** Extract the substring before the first comma with `indexOf` and trim it, rather than splitting the whole header with the backtracking regular expression.

judge_reasoning: The issue identifies a regular-expression denial of service in method-override triggered by crafted X-HTTP-Method-Override header input. It explains catastrophic/backtracking behavior in the header parsing split, causing synchronous event-loop blocking and service degradation—the same vulnerability instance and attack pattern.

detected_issues.title: Failed render requests leave Chrome targets open
detected_issues.body:
Each failed request leaves the target created for it open. An unauthenticated caller can repeatedly request an invalid or unreachable URL; `Page.navigate`/`loadingFailed` rejects, the route returns an error, and no `CDP.Close` runs. Chrome targets then accumulate until the renderer exhausts its available resources.

**Evidence:** `serialize` creates a target at `src/renderer.js:177-180`, but calls `CDP.Close` only after a successful load and evaluation at `src/renderer.js:184-193`; its `catch` at `src/renderer.js:194-195` only rejects. `_loadPage` rejects for navigation and initial-load failures at `src/renderer.js:74` and `src/renderer.js:95-100`. `captureScreenshot` has the same success-only close pattern at `src/renderer.js:201-223`. Both public wildcard routes accept a caller-controlled URL and turn failed serialization into a response at `src/main.js:91-107` and `src/main.js:110-130`; existing tests treat invalid URLs as normal 400 cases at `test/app-test.js:136-146`.

**Impact:** An unauthenticated network caller can cause an unbounded resource leak and deny the rendering service. Under the review policy, this is high: broad service availability impact with recoverability only by restarting/cleaning Chrome, with no in-code target limit.

**Fix:** Always close the created CDP target in a `finally` block (and close/disconnect the client as appropriate), including setup, navigation, evaluation, and screenshot failures.

detected_issues.title: Render URLs inject JavaScript into the loaded page
detected_issues.body:
A percent-encoded quote in the URL becomes a literal quote in `request.params.url` and is interpolated into a single-quoted DevTools expression. For example, a caller can use an allowed-origin URL whose path contains `%27);document.body.innerHTML=1;//`; after Express decodes it, the expression at this line executes the injected statement in the loaded page before that page is returned.

**Preconditions:** `renderOnly` is configured when the impact relies on access to an allowed origin.

**Evidence:** The public render route passes the decoded wildcard parameter unchanged to `serialize` at `src/main.js:91-100`. The renderer navigates that same string at `src/renderer.js:74`, then builds `Runtime.evaluate` source by placing the raw URL inside `'${url}'` at `src/renderer.js:184-189`. The configured restriction is only a prefix test at `src/main.js:65-74`, so an allowed origin plus an attacker-controlled path reaches this code. `injectBaseHref` itself uses `setAttribute`, but that protection is bypassed because its invocation is constructed as source text.

**Impact:** A remote caller can execute arbitrary JavaScript with an allowed site's origin after it loads, including reading same-origin browser-accessible data and sending it to the caller. Under the review policy this is medium: it crosses the configured render-origin boundary, discounted one tier because `renderOnly` is not enabled by default.

**Fix:** Pass the URL as a DevTools call argument or serialize it with `JSON.stringify(url)` when constructing the expression; never interpolate it into a quoted JavaScript literal.

detected_issues.title: Render-only allowlists accept lookalike and redirected hosts
detected_issues.body:
The configured domain restriction authorizes a textual prefix, while the new renderer gives that string directly to Chrome. With the documented `renderOnly: ["https://allowed.example"]`, an unauthenticated caller can request `https://allowed.example.evil/` or `https://allowed.example@evil.example/`; both pass `startsWith`, but Chrome navigates to the attacker-selected authority. An approved URL can also redirect to an unapproved destination because no later request is checked.

**Preconditions:** The deployment configures `renderOnly` (the documented configuration omits a trailing slash).

**Evidence:** `isRestricted` only tests `url.startsWith(...)` at `src/main.js:65-74`, and both wildcard routes authorize once before passing the value to the renderer at `src/main.js:91-100` and `src/main.js:110-119`. The added `_loadPage` directly navigates it at `src/renderer.js:74`; its network handlers only track load state and never validate request or redirect destinations at `src/renderer.js:79-100`. The documented example uses a domain-only prefix in `README.md:197-199`.

**Impact:** A caller can bypass the operator's render-origin boundary and use the renderer to reach an unapproved host, defeating a control intended to limit SSRF and browser access. Under the review policy this is medium: it crosses the configured boundary, discounted one tier because the restriction is opt-in.

**Fix:** Parse URLs and compare normalized scheme, host, and effective port to an allowlist before navigation; enforce the same policy for every redirect/request Chrome makes.

detected_issues.title: DevTools setup failures leave render requests pending
detected_issues.body:
When a DevTools setup command fails, the request never settles. The `async` executor passed to `new Promise` returns its own rejected promise, which the Promise constructor ignores; because the failed await is outside a `try` that calls the outer `reject`, the route remains awaiting it indefinitely.

**Evidence:** `_loadPage` awaits the CDP enable calls without error forwarding at `src/renderer.js:42-51`. Both public methods use the same pattern and await `CDP.New`/`CDP` before their local error handling at `src/renderer.js:177-183` and `src/renderer.js:201-216`; screenshot metric calls are also outside that handler at `src/renderer.js:211-214`. The routes await these promises without a response timeout at `src/main.js:97-107` and `src/main.js:116-131`. This is reachable after the unauthenticated `/_ah/stop` handler kills Chrome at `src/main.js:136-139`: the subsequent `CDP.New` rejects against the stale port, but the affected renderer promise stays pending.

**Impact:** A remote caller can retain pending Express requests after a Chrome failure, consuming service connections rather than receiving a bounded error. Under the review policy this is medium: the impact is broad but recoverable, and it relies on a Chrome outage (which the existing public stop route can trigger).

**Fix:** Do not use async Promise executors. Make these methods `async`, or wrap all setup work in `try`/`catch` that rejects the outer promise, and use `finally` for cleanup.

detected_issues.title: Page console logs can finish rendering before pending work
detected_issues.body:
A rendered page can log the marker text while it still has work in flight, and Rendertron returns the incomplete page as a successful result. This is not limited to the injected completion listener: `Console.messageAdded` accepts any console message with that text.

**Evidence:** The injected listener logs `Rendering complete` only after a `render-complete` event (src/renderer.js:35-40), but the handler at src/renderer.js:148-152 calls `budgetExpired()` for any matching page console message. Unlike the virtual-time handler, that path does not check `pageLoadEventFired` or `outstandingRequests` (src/renderer.js:127-136). `budgetExpired()` resolves immediately (src/renderer.js:115-125), so `serialize()` serializes (src/renderer.js:185-194) or `captureScreenshot()` captures (src/renderer.js:217-222) before a pending fetch or DOM update finishes. A page that logs this common status text from `load` before a fetch reproduces the issue.

**Impact:** One render can return incomplete HTML or a screenshot as HTTP 200. When caching is enabled, the incorrect 200 response may be stored for a day (src/cache.js:32-45, src/cache.js:94-99). This is contained and recoverable, so severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Signal completion through a unique page binding or a value unavailable to ordinary page console output; do not treat arbitrary console text as the `render-complete` event.

detected_issues.title: Serialized pages lose their doctype and enter quirks mode
detected_issues.body:
Rendered HTML drops the source document's doctype. Browsers that later load the returned page therefore enter quirks mode even when the source used standards mode.

**Evidence:** `stripPage()` removes only scripts and HTML imports (src/renderer.js:159-165). The serializer returns `document.firstElementChild.outerHTML` (src/renderer.js:190), which is the `<html>` element and cannot include its preceding `DocumentType` node. `main.js` sends that value unchanged (src/main.js:99-100). Thus a source beginning `<!doctype html>` produces a response without that declaration; loading it changes `document.compatMode` from `CSS1Compat` to `BackCompat` and can alter layout.

**Impact:** This affects the rendered output for documents with a doctype; retrying does not repair it, but the caller can recover by using the source. The effect is limited to one rendered response, so severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Prefix the serialized HTML with `document.doctype` (when present), or serialize the document in a way that preserves the doctype.

detected_issues.title: Meta status codes can produce a response with no final status
detected_issues.body:
A page can supply an invalid final HTTP status through `render:status_code`. In particular, `100` produces an interim response with no following final response, so the client does not receive the rendered document.

**Preconditions:** The requester can render a page that controls its HTML (or controls an allowed origin when `renderOnly` is enabled).

**Evidence:** `getStatusCode()` uses permissive `parseInt()` with no range validation (src/renderer.js:27-31). For a normally successful page containing `<meta name="render:status_code" content="100">`, `_loadPage()` replaces the initial 200 with 100 (src/renderer.js:86-90, src/renderer.js:115-122), and `main.js` passes it straight to Express (src/main.js:91-100). Node treats 1xx as informational and suppresses the body; this handler supplies no final status. Numeric prefixes such as `404junk` are also accepted even though they are not HTTP status codes.

**Impact:** A requester can make a render request for a controlled page hang or fail instead of returning its rendered output. The effect is limited to that request and is recoverable, so severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Accept only a complete, valid final response status (normally 200–599) before replacing the original status; otherwise retain the original status or return a clear error.

judge_reasoning: None of the reported issues concerns exposing node_modules/package.json files or leaking server absolute paths via the _where attribute. They address rendering completion, doctype serialization, and HTTP status handling.

detected_issues.title: Whitespace-only `%o` values block the event loop quadratically
detected_issues.body:
An attacker can block a Node process when an enabled debug call formats attacker-controlled data with `%o`. A whitespace-only string has no newline, so the required `\n` never matches: at each character position the leading `\s*` consumes and backtracks over the rest of the string before the global search tries the next position. The work is quadratic and runs synchronously on the event loop.

**Preconditions:** An application enables the namespace through `DEBUG` and passes request-controlled data to a `%o` debug call.

**Evidence:** `src/debug.js:93-108` dispatches `%o` with the caller value when the namespace is enabled, and the new formatter at `src/node.js:83-86` inspects it then applies `/\s*\n\s*/g`. With `DEBUG=attack` and `DEBUG_MAX_STRING_LENGTH=null`, formatting 40,000 spaces took about 1.26 seconds and 80,000 took about 5.27 seconds (roughly four times the work for twice the input). The base commit has no `src/node.js`, so this path becomes reachable through this change; `src/index.js:6-10` selects it in Node.

**Impact:** A remote caller can repeatedly stall a service that logs its input in an enabled namespace. This is a recoverable availability loss across the request boundary; under the review policy it is discounted from high to **medium** because enabling `DEBUG` is non-default.

**Fix:** Normalize lines without the ambiguous adjacent quantifiers, for example split on `\n`, trim each line, and join with one space.

detected_issues.title: Replacement-token separators corrupt converted names
detected_issues.body:
A documented string separator containing replacement tokens is not emitted literally. For example, `decamelize('fooBar', '$&')` returns `fooobbar` rather than `foo$&bar`, because `$&` is expanded to the matched `oB` while performing the first replacement. Callers that use a literal `$`-based separator therefore receive corrupted converted names.

**Evidence:** The API accepts `separator` as an unrestricted `string` (`readme.md:29-38`). `index.js:6` preserves the supplied value, then `index.js:7` concatenates it into a `String#replace` replacement template. In that template, `$&` means the full match; running the public export with `'fooBar', '$&'` reproduces the result above.

**Impact:** Each affected conversion has incorrect output until retried with a different separator. This is contained and transient, so severity is **info** under the review policy.

**Fix:** Supply the separator through a replacement callback (or otherwise quote replacement-template tokens), while using an independently escaped value only for the dynamically constructed regular expression.

detected_issues.title: Failed SQLcl uploads are reported as successful
detected_issues.body:
`spawnSync` returns a result instead of throwing when SQLcl is missing or exits with an error, but this path always prints `Files were uploaded successfully.`. Thus a normal call with a nonempty directory can report that deployment completed when SQLcl was absent, could not connect, or rejected the upload.

**Evidence:** `spawnSync()` is called at `index.js:74-79`; its `error` and exit `status` are not checked, and execution unconditionally reaches the success log at `index.js:81-82`. The documented default executable is `sql` (`readme.md:33-37`), so an absent SQLcl installation reaches this path.

**Impact:** The affected caller receives a false deployment result and may proceed with a release whose static assets were never uploaded. This is contained and recoverable by fixing SQLcl and retrying, so it is low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Treat a non-null `childProcess.error` or a nonzero `childProcess.status` as failure; only emit the success message after a zero exit status.

detected_issues.title: Invalid destinations upload assets as application files
detected_issues.body:
A value outside the documented `destination` choices is accepted and is uploaded as application static files. For example, a caller that supplies `destination: 'workspcae'` expecting workspace assets instead selects `wwv_flow_api.create_app_static_file`, so the whole directory is deployed to the application scope instead of failing validation.

**Evidence:** The only validation for `destination` is the plugin-name check at `index.js:30-32`. The `default` branch at `index.js:50-62` labels every unrecognized value as an application upload, and the value is forwarded at `index.js:64-71`. `lib/distUpload.js:55-96` sends every value other than `theme`, `workspace`, or `plugin` to the application-static-file API. The documented choices are limited to `application`, `workspace`, `theme`, and `plugin` (`readme.md:40`).

**Impact:** A typo can place release assets in the wrong APEX storage scope rather than stopping the deployment. The effect is confined to the caller's selected application and is recoverable by removing the misplaced files and retrying, so it is low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Validate `destination` against the documented choices before launching SQLcl, and reject other values instead of taking the application fallback.
